Things you need to know about Superloop nbn plans

Why can’t I start at 2 Gbps right away?

To access 2 Gbps speeds, all premises need upgraded hardware, specifically, a new nbn connection box that supports ultra-fast fibre. This is part of nbn’s infrastructure upgrade process to ensure you can enjoy life at ultra-fast speeds.Your current connection box can handle 1 Gbps, so we’ll start you there while nbn schedules a technician to install the upgrade. Once the upgraded box is in place, you’ll be automatically switched over to the full 2 Gbps plan.

                  Network Termination Device

                  The nbn™ Network Termination Device (NTD) is the connection box that links your premises to the nbn access network. Its appearance may vary depending on the available technology at your address, and it requires power to function. Please note, the NTD is separate from your modem (whether supplied by us or BYO). If the NTD is missing, there may be a delay in activation until it is delivered.

                    What’s a speed tier and how does it work?

                    Speed tiers represent the theoretical maximum speed available to your home. However, the actual speeds you experience may vary depending on factors such as network congestion, in-home conditions (e.g., multiple users streaming or gaming), and the placement of your modem (placing it in a cupboard is not recommended). For further information, refer to TES or our About nbn speeds section below.

                      What are Typical Evening Speeds (TES)?

                      Typical Evening Speeds refer to the average speeds you can expect between 7pm and 11pm. These speeds are not guaranteed, and past performance is not an indication of future speeds. Several factors can affect your connection quality and speed, including your access technology (modem/router), network demand (the number of users and their activities), local internet traffic (from nearby homes), and the condition of your physical line (e.g., old or poorly maintained lines).

                        How do you get Superfast and Lightspeed nbn speeds?

                        If you’ve got a Fibre to the Premises (FTTP) or Hybrid Fibre Coaxial (HFC) connection, you’re already ahead of the game. Why? Because you’re eligible for our Superfast and Lightspeed tiers. Here’s a couple of things to keep in mind about these plans:

                        1. Download speeds can vary depending on the time of day, so we recommend using Typical Evening Speed as a guide to what you can expect.

                        2. To get the most out of our Superfast and Lightspeed plans, we highly recommend using a Superloop-supplied modem because they are preconfigured to work perfectly with our network, so you can set it up quickly and get the best speeds possible.

                          What to know about FTTN/B speeds

                          Your maximum speed can only be confirmed once your FTTN, FTTB, or FTTC service is set up and tested. If your line can’t handle the speed you’ve chosen, we’ll help you switch to a more suitable plan and credit any difference, as long as you let us know within 3 months. Some lines might struggle with higher speeds (like FTTC over 100Mbps or FTTN/FTTB above 50Mbps), so the best way to know for sure is to get your service up and running.

                            Medical disclaimer

                            Your nbn service will not function during a power outage, meaning services reliant on the internet, such as VoIP, will be unavailable. However, FTTP-enabled properties can maintain UNI-V functionality if an nbn battery backup is installed and operational.

                            If you have a Back to Base Security Alarm or Medi-Alert connected to your phone service, it's essential to check with your provider to ensure compatibility with the nbn service and explore available alternatives. This must be arranged before transitioning to the nbn network to ensure your alarm remains functional.

                                      Avoiding scams

                                      While scams are not a new phenomenon, digital scams have been on the rise in Australia in recent years. Using a wide range of methods and channels, scammers have become increasingly adept at accessing individuals' money and personal information, often going so far as to impersonate legitimate government bodies, businesses, and organisations.

                                      We've created this guide to educate you on scams and provide tips on how to protect yourself and your family.

                                        About nbn speeds

                                        About nbn speeds

                                        Connection technology and selected speed tier

                                        The connection technology used to link your premises to the Superloop nbn network may vary depending on your specific address. Each technology offers a different theoretical maximum speed, and within each type, multiple speed tiers may be available. The table below outlines the various nbn connection types.

                                        Connection technology  Description
                                        Fibre to the Premises (FTTP) Optical Fibre runs from the internet and Superloop's network direct to your premises.
                                        Hybrid Fibre Coaxial (HFC)Optical Fibre runs from the internet and Superloop's network to a node in your street or nearby street. An existing ‘pay TV’ or coaxial cable then runs from the node to your premises.
                                        Fibre to the Node (FTTN)Optical Fibre runs from the internet and Superloop's network to a node in your street or nearby street. Copper wires (usually the existing phone line) runs from the node to your premises.
                                        Fibre to the Curb (FTTC)Optical Fibre runs from the internet and Superloop's network to a pit in the footpath close to your premises. Copper wires (usually the existing phone line) runs from the pit to your premises.
                                        Fibre to the Building (FTTB)Generally used in apartment blocks or similar type of buildings. Optical Fibre runs from the internet and Superloop's network to a node in your building's communications equipment room. A copper cable runs from the node to your premises.
                                        Fixed WirelessTypically used in circumstances where the distance between premises is large. A fixed antenna on your roof receives a signal from a wireless tower.
                                         SatelliteA satellite dish is installed on your premises and receives a signal from a satellite.

                                          The connection to your area and premises

                                          Several factors specific to your access line can impact your internet speeds, including:

                                            • The type of technology used (FTTN, FTTB, HFC, or Fixed Wireless)
                                            • The length and quality of the copper or coaxial line from your premises to the node
                                            • The condition of your internal cabling and the layout within your home
                                            • External electrical interference, both inside and outside your property
                                            • Network conditions such as the Co-existence period
                                            • Weather conditions, including extreme heat, heavy rain, and any obstacles affecting signal strength for Fixed Wireless connections

                                            Each of these factors can influence your overall internet performance, so it's important to consider them when assessing your connection speed.

                                            FTTN/B/C co-existence period and potential speed impact

                                              Co-existence refers to the period during which your nbn FTTN/B/C service, which partly relies on the copper network, operates alongside other services using the same copper line from your local exchange to your premises. These co-existing services include:

                                              • ADSL, ADSL2, ADSL2+
                                              • SHDSL
                                              • ISDN
                                              • Any other Copper ULL based service other than VDSL

                                              The Co-existence period starts when you can first access an nbn FTTN/B/C service and continues until all legacy services are disconnected from your local exchange.

                                              During this period, the presence of legacy services can impact the performance of your nbn FTTN/B/C service in the following ways:

                                              • Cross talk
                                              • Downstream power back-off applied by nbn
                                              • Other temporary measures taken by nbn to manage interactions between the performance of your nbn FTTN/B/C service and Co-existing services.

                                              NBN Co considers your nbn FTTN/B/C service within specification if, during the Co-existence period, your speed is above 12Mbps down and 1Mbps up, and after the Co-existence period ends, speeds are above 25Mbps down and 5Mbps up, regardless of the speed tier ordered.

                                              While Superloop strives to deliver the highest speed possible, factors outside of our control can affect performance. We always recommend using the Superloop supplied modem for nbn FTTN/B/C services to ensure you get the best possible speeds and support.

                                              Network management and congestion

                                              During busy times, broadband speeds can drop as more people use the network at once. In these moments, the overall network capacity tends to have a greater impact on your speed than your chosen access line or speed tier.

                                              To handle congestion, Superloop uses tools to prioritise certain types of traffic. For example, during peak usage, we may prioritise voice calls (VoIP) and video streaming data, which require stable speeds to work well, over general browsing or downloading. Activities like software updates and file-sharing, which can overload the network, are typically given lower priority during these times.

                                              Your internet speed can also be affected by where the content you're accessing is hosted. If the server you're downloading from is congested or has limited capacity, it can cause delays, even with a fast home connection. Additionally, if the server is overseas, international network congestion could slow things down further.
